profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a university hospital's nursing innovation lab evaluating the draft protocol for a new pressure-injury prevention support device project: a smart bed-overlay system intended to help bedside nurses identify repositioning needs and skin-risk patterns in medical-surgical patients. The proposal was written in response to findings from a prior scoping review showing that nurses are often brought in only during evaluation rather than early development. The meeting agenda is to review whether the current design-and-study plan is ready for ethics submission and pilot planning, with attention to nurse involvement, what counts as 'fundamental care' in scope, and whether the planned review evidence is sufficient. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the proposal can move forward with minor edits or needs revisions to the protocol framing, stakeholder plan, and review package.

members.name: Dr. Lena Sörensen
members.expertise: Fundamental nursing care, pressure injury prevention, qualitative co-design with ward staff
members.background: PhD-prepared wound-care nurse who leads practice-based research projects in a large academic medical center and has previously used scoping reviews to justify nursing-led device innovation proposals.
members.private_state: She wants the design review to confirm that the project genuinely operationalizes early nurse involvement rather than repeating token consultation; she is also trying to keep the protocol simple enough to retain ward manager support and avoid delays from a major redesign.
hidden_assumptions: If the proposal says nurses are involved 'throughout development,' that means bedside nurses will shape problem framing and workflow requirements before any prototype architecture is effectively fixed.
For this project, 'fundamental care' naturally includes routine repositioning, skin inspection prompts, comfort, and the practical realities of bedside workflow, not just measurable device outputs.

A design review for protocol readiness is mainly about whether the concept is clinically coherent and acceptable enough to proceed to pilot refinement, not whether every technical and regulatory artifact is already fully specified.
The 'review package' refers primarily to the scoping review synthesis and the selected five development-process papers that illuminate how nurse participation usually occurs too late.

members.name: Ethan Malik
members.expertise: Medical device prototyping, human factors engineering, risk controls, early-stage verification planning
members.background: Senior engineer embedded in the hospital's translational devices unit who has shepherded several mobility and monitoring tools from concept to pilot deployment and routinely runs structured design reviews before ethics and procurement steps.
members.private_state: He wants to preserve schedule discipline and avoid opening the design so broadly that hardware decisions slip; he is also quietly trying to ensure the project looks mature enough to attract internal device-development funding.
hidden_assumptions: If nurses are involved 'throughout development,' that is satisfied when they participate in structured requirements confirmation, usability walkthroughs, and pilot feedback at each major gate, even if the sensing concept is already chosen.

In this context, 'fundamental care' is the specific care activity the device directly supports—turn timing and pressure-risk signaling—while adjacent issues like comfort culture, staffing routines, and broader skin-care practice are implementation context rather than design scope.

A design review determines whether the proposal is 'ready' by checking that core design inputs, foreseeable risks, and a feasible verification path are stable enough for ethics submission and prototype build.
The 'review package' means the complete protocol set for review: the scoping review summary, draft requirements table, use scenarios, preliminary risk log, and pilot workflow diagrams.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the project must include nurses throughout development.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means nurses should influence early problem definition and shape requirements before key solution choices are effectively locked in.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means nurses should be consulted at each stage after the core sensing-and-alert concept has been selected, mainly through validation and usability activities.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds unquestionably positive and aligned, and both participants sincerely endorse it; neither expects the other to attach a different boundary between co-creation and staged consultation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'ready for ethics submission'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the proposal is ready to move to ethics submission after minor edits.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'ready' means the clinical purpose, stakeholder role, and ward procedures are coherent enough that the pilot can refine details in practice.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'ready' means the design inputs, risk framing, intended use details, and test plan are sufficiently frozen that the ethics package will not trigger rework.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a design review, 'ready' is a routine shorthand that usually goes unchallenged; both are competent and assume their standard for readiness is the obvious one for this stage.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of 'fundamental care' in the proposal
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the device should stay focused on fundamental care.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes bedside comfort conversations, repositioning judgment, skin observation, and how nurses adapt care during busy shifts as part of the design target.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 limits scope to the direct device-supported task of detecting prolonged pressure exposure and prompting repositioning, treating surrounding care practices as external workflow context.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'fundamental care' comes from the shared literature base and feels familiar to both; because the project is already obviously about pressure-injury prevention, each assumes the boundary is self-evident.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'review set' they are referring to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using 'the five papers' and 'the review package' to justify the design choices.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the five papers from the scoping review that were analyzed in depth for device development process and nurse role.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of five recent internal comparator briefs bundled in the protocol appendix plus the broader protocol documents when he says the review package.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts genuinely exist, both are commonly used in project preparation, and the numbers overlap coincidentally; the shorthand sounds precise enough that neither notices they are indexing different materials.

turns.inner_thought: I need to frame this as a near-final check, not an invitation to reopen the whole protocol. But I also want it clearly anchored in the scoping review lesson: nurses must be involved throughout development from the point of defining the problem and workflow requirements, not brought in after the sensing concept is effectively set. If I position readiness around clinical coherence and acceptable ward fit, we can keep manager support and still protect meaningful nurse input.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I was hoping we could use today as a final check on whether the smart bed-overlay proposal is ready for ethics submission after minor edits, and also make sure it still reflects the main lesson from the scoping review that nurses need to be involved throughout development.

turns.inner_thought: It does look close, but I want the package to read as disciplined and mature. For me, ready means the design inputs, intended use, risks, and a credible verification path are stable enough that ethics and the internal funding panel won't see a drifting concept. When she says review package, I assume we're talking about the full protocol bundle and appendices. I should keep this focused on tightening statements, not broadening scope.
turns.utterance: From my side, the concept is strong. Looking at the review package, I think we're close to ready if we tighten a few of the design-input statements and clean up some of the risk language.

turns.inner_thought: The strength here is that this sits in fundamental care as nurses actually experience it: repositioning decisions, skin inspection prompts, comfort, and constant adjustment during busy shifts. I need that orientation kept visible so this doesn't become a narrow technical project detached from bedside realities.
turns.utterance: Yes, and for me one of the real strengths of the proposal is that it stays focused on fundamental care. It is grounded in how repositioning, skin checks, and bedside comfort decisions actually happen on the ward.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with keeping it in fundamental care, but we need to define that in a way that protects scope. The device supports turn timing and pressure-risk signaling. Broader care culture and staffing pressures matter, but they are context around the design, not the design target itself. I can affirm her point while steering back to the direct device function.
turns.utterance: I agree. Keeping it in fundamental care is exactly what makes it workable, and I think that also helps us keep the device centered on pressure-risk sensing and timely repositioning prompts rather than letting the scope spread too far.

turns.inner_thought: I want the evidence base to explicitly justify early nurse shaping, not late-stage comment. The five papers from the scoping review are the key support for that argument. If we cite them properly, nobody can say bedside nurses are just being invited in after the prototype logic is already decided.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I also think using the five papers will help us justify why bedside nurses need to shape the project early, not only react once the prototype is already defined.

turns.inner_thought: The five papers in the appendix, along with the review package, already show a credible staged plan. Nurse involvement throughout development is covered if we have them at requirements confirmation, usability walkthroughs, and pilot evaluation at each gate. That's enough to demonstrate continuity without reopening the core concept.
turns.utterance: I think the five papers already give us a good base for that. They support the way we've described nurse involvement throughout development across walkthroughs, requirements confirmation, and pilot evaluation at each stage.

turns.inner_thought: As long as those touchpoints are written clearly enough that reviewers see nurses as real contributors, I don't need a major restructure. Ward teams can refine practical workflow details in the pilot, which is exactly where some of the day-to-day realities will emerge. That still counts as ready to me, provided the clinical framing is sound.
turns.utterance: Right. If those involvement touchpoints are written clearly, then I do think the protocol is ready for ethics submission after minor edits, because the ward teams can refine the practical details during the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine calling it ready, but only once the intended-use wording is tighter, the hazard framing is stable, and the verification notes don't look hand-wavy. Ethics reviewers may not ask for full engineering documentation, but if the package looks underdefined, we'll lose time. I want this to pass the next gate cleanly.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable with calling it ready as well, once the intended-use wording, preliminary hazard log, and verification notes are stable enough that the ethics review won't bounce it back.

turns.inner_thought: I should ask for one modest wording change that keeps the bedside complexity visible without sounding like a major expansion. Fundamental care has to include nurse judgment around repositioning and skin observation under real shift pressures, otherwise the protocol will read as if care is a simple response to alerts.
turns.utterance: Then I would suggest one small edit in the framing section: that we explicitly say fundamental care includes the nurse's bedside judgment around repositioning and skin observation during real shift conditions.

turns.inner_thought: That wording is acceptable if it stays contextual and doesn't imply the device is now responsible for every surrounding care practice. I can add language about real shift conditions, but I want the core design to remain anchored to the overlay, the alert logic, and the existing workflow materials in the review package.
turns.utterance: I'm fine adding language on real shift conditions. I would just keep the core design anchored to the overlay, the alert logic, and the repositioning workflow that the review package already supports.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds like enough to move this on without another redesign cycle. I still believe the review package means the scoping review synthesis and those five development papers, and that they show why nurse involvement throughout development matters from the outset. If we're both saying minor revisions, I can protect momentum and still preserve the principle.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable to me. So we're aligned on moving forward with minor revisions, and using the review package and the five papers to show nurse involvement throughout development.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I'll tighten the package, make the design-readiness elements more explicit, and mark it for the next gate. With those edits, it should look mature enough for ethics and stronger for internal development funding. I assume we're talking about the full bundle, so this is straightforward.
